title: Cabaness v. Thomas
lead: An employee alleged years of intimidation despite a city manual’s protective promises, producing different results for his contract, tort, and constructive-termination claims.

actors.name: Kipp Cabaness
actors.role: Bountiful Light & Power foreman who resigned after alleged mistreatment

actors.name: Municipal employer
actors.role: Issuer of the personnel manual and contract defendant

proceedings: District court: summary judgment for defendants, formation cross-motion and postjudgment evidence rejected.
Utah Supreme Court: contract formation established; contract and Thomas tort claims returned for further proceedings; other dismissals affirmed.
limits: The April 23, 2010 amended opinion controls this account. It establishes formation, not breach or damages. Emotional contract damages require proof of contemplation and foreseeability; historical immunity law is not certified as current.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The city promises protection from harassment while workplace problems accumulate
sections.cue: Introduce the employment relationship and actual manual limits.
paragraphs: Kipp Cabaness worked for Bountiful Light & Power from March 1978 to January 2004 and was a line-working foreman from 1984. Operations superintendent Brent Thomas supervised him but could not fire him; director Clifford Michaelis could. Cabaness was undisputedly a regular employee covered by the city personnel manual.

The manual disclaimed contractual obligations about salary, salary ranges, movement within those ranges, and benefits. Other provisions promised not to tolerate harassing, intimidating, offensive, or hostile conduct, prohibited threats and violence, and barred harassment or retaliation for good-faith use of its procedures.

For summary-judgment review, employee testimony described years of Thomas’s profanity, humiliation, needless work changes, threats, and disregard of electrical safety. Examples included refusing a safety ground on a high-voltage line, cutting safety meetings short, avoidable rain work, and mockery of personal matters. In July 2003, he allegedly ordered jackhammer work near live equipment despite warnings; it stopped without injury. Cabaness was on medical leave and learned of that episode later. These accounts supported review of whether trial was needed, not final liability findings.

sections.title: Medical leave, complaints, and resignation lead to several legal theories
sections.cue: Trace the factual and procedural sequence.
paragraphs: Cabaness received diagnoses of workplace-related depression in 1997 and 2003. After medically supported summer 2003 leave, Thomas allegedly singled him out publicly and threatened dismissal despite knowing of his depression. Employees repeatedly complained to Michaelis. A 1997 response could reasonably be heard as threatening termination for further complaints, though Michaelis disputed that meaning. An investigation interviewing fifteen employees eventually warned Thomas to stop intimidation.

Cabaness resigned in January 2004. Nearly all Thomas’s crew left between summer 2003 and spring 2004, primarily because of the alleged conduct. Cabaness sued Thomas and Michaelis for intentional infliction of emotional distress and the employer for breach of the manual and wrongful termination.

The district court granted defense summary judgment, denied Cabaness’s cross-motion on contract formation, and rejected postjudgment affidavits from two city employees about intent to create a contract. The Utah Supreme Court reviewed legal summary-judgment questions for correctness and evidentiary exclusions for abuse of discretion. It refused to strike Cabaness’s appellate brief: despite occasional emotional bias, factual assertions and good-faith legal arguments had adequate record and authority support.

sections.title: Evidence and timing narrow but do not eliminate the tort claim
sections.cue: Keep the separate evidentiary rulings straight.
paragraphs: The two postjudgment formation affidavits stayed excluded. The employer’s answer had denied a contract, so due diligence required obtaining that evidence before judgment. The manual itself could still establish formation. Knighton’s affidavit contained admissible personal observations of Thomas’s treatment despite some conclusory statements; alone it did not establish the tort. The court left the Hawks report’s admissibility unresolved because the outcome did not depend on it. Safety-committee factual findings qualified under the public-records hearsay exception.

For an alleged continuing pattern of intentional infliction, the court held limitations ran from the last injury or cessation of conduct, permitting recovery for the whole course. It did not require uncertainty about the first onset of severe distress. Exposure ended with the January 2, 2004 resignation, making the March suit timely. The rule concerned this tort, not automatic extension to nuisance or trespass.

Conduct outside Cabaness’s presence required particularly compelling circumstances, including intent to injure him while absent. No direct evidence showed the jackhammer incident intended such injury, so exclusion from this tort theory was proper. The amended opinion expressly preserved that incident and other outside-presence conduct for the contract claim.

sections.title: Thomas faces trial, while the theory against Michaelis fails
sections.cue: Explain why the supervisors had different outcomes.
paragraphs: The court declined to extend intentional-infliction liability to Michaelis merely for failing to curb someone else’s conduct. Cabaness had not persuasively supported that doctrinal extension. It did not deny broader approaches elsewhere, but affirmed dismissal on this presentation.

Thomas’s alleged pattern warranted trial. Ordinary insults or unfair treatment alone were insufficient, yet persistent humiliation combined with threats, deliberately stressful arrangements, safety disregard, and renewed mistreatment after known medical problems could reasonably be outrageous and intolerable. Because reasonable minds could differ, summary judgment could not resolve that element against Cabaness. The court did not find every tort element proved.

sections.title: The limited disclaimer leaves enforceable protective promises
paragraphs: Although public employment ordinarily arose from statute, government could voluntarily assume added contractual duties. Definite communicated manual promises could form a unilateral contract accepted and supported by continued service. Formation often involved factual issues, but the parties relied on the manual and stipulated on cross-motions that material formation facts were undisputed.

The disclaimer covered specified compensation and benefits rather than every obligation. Alongside it, affirmative promises against harassment, intimidation, and hostility objectively manifested additional duties. The relevant provisions created a contract as a matter of law with an implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing. Other policy or expectation language did not automatically become contractual.

The governing pre-July-2004 immunity statute waived immunity for any contractual obligations. An emotional-anguish exception in a separate negligence waiver did not carry over into the unqualified contract waiver. Other-waiver precedents involved negligence, and amendments expressly incorporated exceptions elsewhere but not here. This was a genuine contract claim, not a relabeled tort. The court also corrected an earlier appellate rationale: where no waiver applied, general governmental-function immunity, not an imported negligence exception, explained immunity. It observed that the 2008 renumbered legislation would yield a very similar analysis and result.

sections.title: Emotional damages remain possible upon proof, not automatically awarded
sections.cue: Explain the conditional contract remedy and failed termination claim.
paragraphs: Ordinary commercial disappointment generally did not support emotional damages. Drawing on Beck, its insurance-contract decision, and personal-contract authorities, the court allowed the possibility where such harm was foreseeable and explicitly within the parties’ contemplation at formation. The agreement’s language, nature, and reasonable expectations controlled; a tort finding against a supervisor was not required.

Promises protecting employees from harassment and a hostile workplace addressed mental concerns and could support that inference. The amended opinion nevertheless remanded whether these parties actually contemplated emotional damages and whether recovery was appropriate. Formation was settled, but breach and necessary damages proof were not.

The manual did not limit termination procedures or require cause. Neither side invoked a statutory at-will exception, and Cabaness admitted not pleading a clear, substantial public-policy violation. A hostile environment causing resignation could support consequential contract damages without satisfying his separate wrongful-constructive-termination claim. Its dismissal was affirmed. The court’s expressed doubt about fitting constructive departure into the specific contractual-procedures exception did not categorically decide every future constructive-termination case.

sections.title: The amended decision returns only the surviving claims
sections.cue: Finish with alignment and the dissent’s limited explanation.
paragraphs: In the April 23, 2010 amended opinion, Justice Parrish, joined by Chief Justice Durham, Associate Chief Justice Durrant, and Justice Nehring, affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded. The contract claim and intentional-infliction claim against Thomas could proceed. Dismissals of the tort claim against Michaelis and the separate constructive-termination claim remained effective.

Justice Wilkins would affirm all district-court rulings. His brief dissent rejected extending Beck beyond insurance and considered the manual language insufficient to create a contract, without extended separate treatment of the other issues. The majority awarded no damages and did not establish breach on the disputed record.
